clue.text: Where paper starts from, as the adage has it

annotationWithheld.why: Where paper starts from, as the adage has it (8): MASTHEAD is the title block where a newspaper's front page starts, but no reading found for 'as the adage has it' (ASTHEAD sits in 'as the adage' yet nothing gives M)
annotationWithheld.clue: Where paper starts from, as the adage has it

clue.text: Saw one's sweetheart achieve best result possible

parts.note: a saw is an old saying, a maxim
one is, written as I plus S, gives IS
the heart of the word sweet is its middle letter, E

explanation.surface: Someone sees their beloved and so gets the best outcome imaginable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past of 'see' but is the noun for a proverb. 'one's' is read as 'one is', giving IS, and 'heart' takes E, the middle of 'sweet'.
explanation.definitionFit: To maximise is to make as large or effective as possible, getting the greatest outcome.

clue.text: Short suit and vest being worn

parts.note: a singlet is a sleeveless vest
clothes being worn are on

explanation.surface: A description of an outfit: shorts, a suit, a vest worn together.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge a short suit is a holding of very few cards; a holding of just one card in a suit is the term here. 'Vest' is the British word for an undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games a lone card in a suit is called by this name, the shortest suit possible.

clue.text: Card games for the crew

explanation.surface: Players settle down to cards on board ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Deals in a card game are each one round of play; deckhands are also called by this word, the workers on a ship.

clue.text: Half of alphabet used in any detailed analysis

indicators.note: the half-alphabet is placed inside the word any

parts.note: taken as written
the first half of the alphabet runs from A to M, written as A TO M

explanation.surface: Only half the letters are used in any thorough study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half of alphabet' is A TO M, the letters from A up to M, which go inside ANY.
explanation.definitionFit: An anatomy of something is a minute examination of its parts, like dissecting a body.

clue.text: Current in a wide part of river

parts.note: a broad is a wide stretch of river, as in the Norfolk Broads

explanation.surface: Water flowing through a wide stretch of river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like flowing water but is the adjective 'in circulation', as a rumour is abroad. The Norfolk Broads are English lakes formed by widened rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Stories that are abroad are circulating widely, generally known or in the air.

clue.text: Under a legal obligation — clear?

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a court order leaves them in the clear.
explanation.definitionFit: A court can order someone to keep the peace or appear later, a binding duty; to clear a fence is to leap across it.

clue.text: European agreements for novelist

parts.note: oui is French for yes
da is Russian for yes

explanation.surface: A writer is signed up after deals across Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: Two foreign words for 'yes' make the pen name of the Victorian writer of Under Two Flags.
explanation.definitionFit: Ouida was the pen name of Maria Louise Ramé, a popular Victorian writer of romances.

clue.text: Keep two little boys together

parts.note: Don is a short form of Donald
Jon is a short form of Jonathan

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep a pair of small children side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like a verb but is the castle tower, and 'little' means each boy's name is shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: A donjon is the central fortified tower of a castle, also called a keep.

clue.text: Fed up about Eastender, it's said

indicators.note: the word sated goes round the letter from East

parts.note: to be fed up, full to the brim, is to be sated
the ender, the last letter, of East is T

explanation.surface: Someone from the East End of London announces they are fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: An EastEnder is a Londoner from the East End, but here it is the end of 'East'. 'Fed up' looks like boredom yet means full.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stated has been declared or put into words, just as said.

clue.text: Nobody returned after vote -— what a gas!

parts.note: a voter marks a cross, X, on the ballot

indicators.note: returned means the word for nobody is read backwards

parts.note: nobody is none

explanation.surface: No-one came back after the election: what a laugh!
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' sends the word for nobody backwards, after the cross on a ballot. 'What a gas!' reads like 'what fun!', but it is literal here.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenon is a noble gas, an inert element used in lamps.

clue.text: Boys like some legends

parts.note: Arthur is a boy's name
Ian is a boy's name

explanation.surface: Lads resemble certain heroes of story.
explanation.walkthrough: Two boys' names put together describe tales of the Round Table.
explanation.definitionFit: Legends of Camelot and the Round Table are about the mythical British king and his knights.

clue.text: Drink extracts maximum from tipster

parts.note: to milk a situation is to get all one can from it
a tout sells racing tips

explanation.surface: A drinker gets the most out of a racing tipster.
explanation.walkthrough: A tout is someone who sells racing tips at a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk stout is a sweet dark beer brewed with lactose, a kind of ale.

clue.text: Awfully 'ard and firm legislator

indicators.note: awfully suggests the letters of the dropped-aitch word are jumbled

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A Cockney grumbles that a lawmaker is terribly hard and unbending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully' scrambles the Cockney 'ard (hard with the H dropped) into DRA, which comes before the firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco was the Athenian lawgiver whose harsh code gave us the word draconian.

clue.text: Content fits awkwardly into report

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go inside the word for report

parts.note: to report something is to say it

indicators.note: awkwardly tells us the letters of fits are rearranged

explanation.surface: Contents are squeezed clumsily into a written report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkwardly' gives TISF, which goes 'into' the word for report after its A. 'Content' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To content someone is to please or gratify them, meeting their wishes.

clue.text: No part of Lovelace's prison block

explanation.surface: A cell block plays no role in a poet's idea of jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovelace wrote that such stone barriers do not a prison make; to obstruct or stall deliberately is also called this.

clue.text: Cut semi-circle. I see

parts.note: the capital D is shaped like half a circle
vide is Latin for see, used in references

explanation.surface: An instruction to cut out a half-circle, with a comment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vide' is the Latin for 'see', as used in footnotes.
explanation.definitionFit: To divide is to split or separate into parts.

clue.text: 'ighly charged feeling between boxers, say, in ruthless contest

indicators.note: the feeling sits between the two dogs

parts.note: boxers are a breed of dog, so two dogs
heat, with the h dropped Cockney style like 'ighly, gives 'eat

explanation.surface: Tension runs high between two fighters in a brutal bout.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped H of 'ighly tells you to drop the H of HEAT too. 'Boxers' are not fighters but dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog-eat-dog world is one of fierce, unscrupulous competition.

clue.text: Girl has loaf, and fruit from tree

parts.note: Hazel is a girl's name
loaf and nut are both slang for the head

explanation.surface: A girl with a loaf of bread and some fruit picked from a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' is slang for the head, from rhyming slang 'loaf of bread', and so is NUT.
explanation.definitionFit: The hazel tree bears small round edible nuts, also called cobnuts.

clue.text: Pass on intelligence, taking spy chief's place

parts.note: taking someone's place is standing in for them
M is the head of the secret service in the Bond stories

explanation.surface: A secret agent passes on news while standing in for the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking ... place' is IN FOR, as a deputy stands in for someone, and M is the spymaster.
explanation.definitionFit: To inform is to tell or give information to someone.

clue.text: Accident is hard to locate in chart

indicators.note: the two pieces are placed inside the word for chart

parts.note: a chart is a map
H stands for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: An accident is hard to pinpoint on a map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is hard' looks like a comment on difficulty, but it gives two pieces that 'locate in' puts inside the chart.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishap is an unlucky event or minor misfortune.

clue.text: Republic needs soldier at a city in Italy

parts.note: Peru is a South American republic
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A country needs its soldier in an Italian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Perugia is the capital of Umbria in central Italy.

clue.text: Easily hit a birdie — follow that!

parts.note: to pat is to hit gently
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A golfer taps in a birdie and challenges a rival to match it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'birdie' is a golf score but here just a bird. The definition is a design or model one is told to follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A pattern is a template or model meant to be copied.

clue.text: Repeated British exclamation of surprise

parts.note: B is short for British
Limey is American slang for a Briton

explanation.surface: A Briton keeps exclaiming in astonishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repeated' tells you British is used twice: once as B, once as LIMEY, slang for a Brit.
explanation.definitionFit: Blimey is a British slang cry of astonishment.

clue.text: Able to move supply? Left with one article

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: Asking if goods can be shifted, with one item left over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a noun for stock but is the adverb from supple, so the definition is moving in a supple way.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithe means flexible and graceful, bending easily.

clue.text: Part of opera to read over endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly drops the last letter of the word for read over

parts.note: to scan a text is to read over it

explanation.surface: Someone glances through part of an opera score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts the final N from SCAN. 'Part' is a role: Floria Tosca is the heroine of Puccini's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosca is the title role, a singer heroine, in Puccini's opera.

clue.text: Conventional and old-fashioned drawing instrument

parts.note: set ways are fixed and conventional
a square is a stuffy, old-fashioned person

explanation.surface: A traditional and dated tool used in technical drawing.
explanation.definitionFit: A set square is a triangular plate used to draw angles in technical drawing.

clue.text: Birds flinch

explanation.surface: Birds shrink back in fear.
explanation.definitionFit: Quail are small game birds; to quail is to recoil or lose courage.

clue.text: Run badly in main games, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests the letters of main games have come out wrong, scrambled

explanation.surface: A team manager blunders in the important matches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges the letters of MAIN GAMES.
explanation.definitionFit: To mismanage is to handle or administer poorly.

clue.text: An American poet: a University study

parts.note: a den is a private study room

explanation.surface: A poet from the States studying at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: W. H. Auden was English-born but became a US citizen in 1946.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was a British-born poet who took US citizenship.

clue.text: Yorkshire opener soon appearing in wisden, say

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, here the start of Yorkshire

parts.note: early means soon, before long

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire opening batsman will soon feature in the cricket almanac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' looks like a cricket batsman but takes the first letter. Wisden is the annual almanac of English cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisden comes out once a year, an annual publication.

clue.text: Sort of movie that's highly enjoyable

definitions.text: Sort of movie that's highly enjoyable

parts.words: Sort of movie that's highly enjoyable
parts.note: a film watched high up, on board an aircraft, is enjoyed at altitude

explanation.surface: Praise for an especially good film.
explanation.definitionFit: Airlines show films to passengers during the journey, entertainment while airborne.
